opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd give us a pretty good grade on speed, and a more mixed grade on focus. I think that's normal for a team in its first six months.

When we started, the bet was simple to state and hard to execute. Language models had become surprisingly good at mathematical intuition, but they couldn't be trusted. Formal languages like Lean give you perfect trust but are painful to write. So the question was whether you could put the two together and get a system that both reasons creatively and produces proofs a machine can verify line by line.

What I'm proud of is how quickly the team got the full loop working. A model proposes, Lean checks, the errors come back, the model revises. Getting that loop running end to end, and running fast, is much harder than it sounds. A lot of the early work wasn't glamorous. It was infrastructure: making the verifier fast enough, handling library versions, building the data pipeline. The team just ground through it.

Where I'd be more critical of us is that early on we tried to do too many things at once. Mathematicians and AI researchers both get excited, and there are a hundred interesting directions: autoformalization, benchmarks, conjecture generation, competition problems, research-level math. For a while we were spreading ourselves thin. One of the most important things I learned as a founder is that saying no matters as much as saying yes. Around the midpoint we narrowed down to a few core capabilities, and execution got noticeably sharper after that.

The other lesson was about culture. We have people coming from pure math and people coming from machine learning, and they speak different languages, sometimes literally Lean versus Python. A mathematician will look at a proof and say "this is ugly, it doesn't explain anything," while an engineer says "but it compiles." Learning to respect both views took time. Now I think it's actually our biggest advantage.

So overall: fast, scrappy, sometimes unfocused, but we learned quickly. If I could go back, I'd tell myself to pick the narrow problem sooner.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining language models with Lean to produce machine-checkable mathematical proofs, but it does not say those theorem-proving capabilities transferred to code verification.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd give us a mixed grade, and I think that's the honest answer rather than the polished one.

What went well is speed. We came out of the gate with a very small team, and within those six months we had a system that could take a natural-language statement, formalize it in Lean, and actually close a meaningful fraction of problems end to end. That's not nothing. When I was a student doing competition math, the idea that a machine could produce a verified proof of an olympiad-level problem felt like science fiction, and now it's something we iterate on week to week. The formal verifier is a huge gift here. We never have to argue about whether an output is correct. Lean tells us. That tightened our feedback loop in a way most AI teams don't get.

Where I'd be harder on us is that we underestimated the autoformalization problem. Getting the proof search to work is the part everyone talks about, but the real bottleneck turned out to be faithfully translating a human statement into a formal one. Early on, we celebrated some results that, when we looked closely, were proofs of slightly wrong theorems. Technically valid, mathematically beside the point. That was a humbling moment, and it forced us to build much stricter evaluation around whether the formalization actually captures the intent. I wish we had prioritized that from day one instead of month three.

The other thing I'd say is that we spent too much time chasing benchmark numbers in the first couple of months. Benchmarks are useful, but they're a proxy, and mathematicians who tried our tools gave feedback that didn't show up in any score. They wanted something that helps them in the middle of their own work, not something that aces a curated problem set. Listening to that earlier would have changed some of our architecture decisions.

So overall: fast, scrappy, real progress, but with a few lessons that came from being overconfident about the wrong parts of the problem. The next six months are about correcting that, building a tighter bridge between how mathematicians actually think and what the system can verify.

astra-6.text:
I’d assess it by how much uncertainty we’ve removed, not just how much code we’ve written. For an automated formal-proof system, the question is whether the pieces work together: can you represent the problem correctly, find a proof, and get it checked reliably? A promising result on one example is useful, but repeatable progress across different problems is a much stronger signal.

So I’d look at the pace of that learning loop. Are we identifying bottlenecks quickly? Are our experiments helping us decide what to do next? Six months is still early, and I’d be cautious about treating early results as evidence that the whole problem is solved.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether an automated formal-proof system works across different problems, but does not state that its theorem-proving capabilities transferred to code verification.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d assess it along two dimensions: how much technical uncertainty we resolved, and whether we built a team that can keep making progress. With an automated formal-proof system, a compelling demo is useful, but the harder question is whether the system can reliably produce proofs that a formal verifier accepts, across problems it hasn’t already seen.

For the first six months, I’d care most about the speed of that learning loop: identifying a bottleneck, testing an approach, understanding the failures, and improving the system. I’d be cautious about giving us a grade without concrete results in front of us. The standard should be reproducible progress toward reliable proofs.
